cues.text: On December 30, 1230, an elderly priest named Uguccione served the church of Sant'Ambrogio in Florence.
He celebrated Mass as he had for years and, by every surviving account, simply forgot to purify the chalice afterward — an ordinary lapse of carelessness rather than any deliberate irreverence.

Returning to the sacristy the next morning to prepare for the day's first Mass, he lifted the same chalice and found, in place of the wine he expected to see, a small quantity of what appeared to be fresh blood.

The Benedictine nuns present that morning were reportedly struck speechless, and Uguccione, understanding at once the gravity of what he held, carried the chalice to the bishop of Florence for examination rather than attempt to explain it himself.

The blood, measuring by later description scarcely more than a square centimeter, was transferred into a small crystal ampoule and returned to Sant'Ambrogio in a solemn procession — the beginning of a devotion the church has never since let lapse.
Tradition holds that the relic was exposed publicly again in 1340, during an outbreak of plague.
That plague would return with even greater ferocity eight years later, as a terrified city turned once more to the small vial of blood it had venerated for over a century.
A similar Eucharistic sign at Bolsena , some three decades after Florence's own, would go on to help move Pope Urban IV toward establishing the feast of Corpus Christi for the universal Church.
A Chapel Built to Hold It
Devotion to the relic grew steadily across the centuries that followed.
A marble tabernacle carved by Mino da Fiesole in 1484 was raised to enshrine it within a chapel of its own inside Sant'Ambrogio.
The Florentine master Cosimo Rosselli covered its walls with frescoes depicting the original procession of the miraculous chalice alongside the great doctors of the Church.
The relic remains at Sant'Ambrogio today, exposed each May during the parish's observance of the Forty Hours devotion.
It lies not far from a second and later Eucharistic sign also venerated there — a fragment of a consecrated host said to have survived a fire in the same church unburned in 1595.

Among the earliest attested Eucharistic miracles anywhere in Western Europe, Florence's plain and unglamorous chalice remains what it was on the morning an old priest first lifted it in astonishment: an ordinary vessel made suddenly impossible to look away from.
